post1.text:
Most leaders at $50M+ companies are not being outpaced by the market. They are being outpaced by themselves.

Here is the uncomfortable truth: the leadership style that got your company to $50 million is often the exact thing preventing it from reaching $500 million. The instincts, the control habits, the decision-making speed that once felt like strengths become bottlenecks at scale.

Entrepreneur.com recently raised a sharp question about whether leaders are actually showing up as the version of themselves their goals require. Most are not. Not because they lack ambition, but because they never updated their leadership operating system to match the company they are now running.

Three things leaders at this stage almost always get wrong: they stay in decisions they should be delegating, they hire for loyalty over capability, and they measure their own performance by activity instead of outcomes.

The company does not have a growth problem. It has a leadership gap problem.

Where is your leadership operating system still running on old code?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company just added three senior executives specifically to support their scaling ambitions in the coaching space.

This is not just a hiring story. This is a scaling strategy story.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern repeatedly with companies pushing past $50M. The leaders who scale successfully do not just hire for today's workload. They hire ahead of the complexity that growth creates. Buffini is not filling seats. They are building a leadership layer that can carry weight the founder or CEO should no longer be carrying alone.

If your org chart still looks like it did when you were half your current size, that is worth examining seriously.

Read the full piece and ask yourself who on your team is scaling with you versus who is becoming a ceiling.

post3.text:
Buffini and Company recently made headlines by bringing in three senior executives to help scale their business. Smart move. And it reflects something Katherine Slain writes about directly in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It, and it opens with a premise that makes most executives uncomfortable: the leader you are right now may not be the leader your next stage of growth requires.

Katherine does not just diagnose the problem. She gives growing companies a clear-eyed framework for understanding what leadership actually has to look like when the complexity of scale kicks in and the old habits stop working.

Hiring new executives is one move. Knowing what kind of leader the organization needs you to become is a different challenge entirely.

Rock Your Business, the second book from Autobahn Consultants by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. But here is the harder truth: thinking about it early is not enough either. You have to build for it from day one.

A recent Entrepreneur piece reinforced something we see constantly with scaling companies: the businesses that command the highest multiples are not the ones that scrambled to clean up their financials before a sale. They are the ones that ran a clean, well-documented, strategically coherent operation for years before a buyer ever showed up.

If you are running a $50M+ business, here is what actually moves your multiple:

1. Recurring revenue beats one-time revenue every time. Buyers pay a premium for predictability.
2. Owner dependency is a valuation killer. If the business cannot run without you for 90 days, that risk gets priced in.
3. Customer concentration above 20% with a single client will shrink your number fast.

The question is not when you plan to exit. It is whether your business today would survive the scrutiny of a serious buyer.

What would a buyer find if they looked at your company right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur makes a case that every founder scaling past $50M needs to hear: your exit plan should be built years before you ever intend to sell.

Autobahn sees this play out constantly. Companies that wait until they are ready to sell spend the final 12 to 24 months in reactive mode, patching financials, fixing leadership gaps, and explaining away customer concentration issues. That is exactly when buyers have the leverage.

The companies that sell on their terms built the exit into the operating model early. Clean books. Transferable systems. A leadership team that does not depend on the founder to function.

If you are between $50M and $500M, the time to think about this is now, not when an offer lands on your desk.

post3.text:
A recent Entrepreneur article on exit planning touches on something our new book addresses head-on.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business, titled "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit" and authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman, goes well beyond the standard advice of getting your financials in order before a sale.

Paul and George work with companies between $50M and $500M and they have seen what actually separates a business that gets a strong multiple from one that leaves money on the table. The answer is not just what your numbers look like. It is how your business is structured, led, and de-risked long before a buyer ever enters the picture.

One thing they make clear: the multiple you receive is not assigned at closing. It is earned over years of intentional decisions.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies don't fail at strategy. They fail at the gap between the conference room and the floor.

Forbes recently dug into why leadership teams consistently miss on execution, and the pattern is familiar: the plan gets built, the deck gets presented, and then real work pulls everyone back to their lanes. Six months later, nothing moved.

Here's what scaling companies get wrong:

1. Strategy and operations are treated as separate jobs. At $50M and beyond, they have to be the same job.

2. Leaders confuse activity with progress. A packed calendar is not a sign the strategy is working.

3. Accountability structures are informal. If the plan lives in a slide deck and not in weekly routines, it will die there.

The businesses that scale past $100M, $200M, and beyond are not smarter. They are more disciplined about connecting decisions at the top to behavior at every level.

So here is the real question: Does your team know what you are actually saying no to this year?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams fall apart when it comes to executing strategy, and it is worth a read if you are running a company in growth mode.

The core problem the article surfaces is not capability. It is alignment. Teams at the top often carry different versions of the same strategy in their heads and never realize it until a critical initiative stalls.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies between $50M and $200M. Growth creates complexity, and complexity quietly fractures the shared understanding that made the company successful in the first place.

The fix is not another planning retreat. It is building execution rhythms that force the strategy into daily and weekly decisions, not just quarterly reviews.

If your leadership team is working hard but the strategy is not moving, this article is a good starting point.

post3.text:
The conversation around strategy execution keeps circling the same problem: leaders build great plans and then watch them stall.

Chapter 3 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head on. The chapter is called "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall, and it draws on real experience running businesses across wildly different industries.

What they found is that the strategic planning lessons that hold up across contexts are not the sophisticated ones. They are the disciplined, unglamorous ones that most leadership teams skip because they feel too simple.

One thing the chapter makes clear: knowing your strategy is not the same as running your business by it. There is a specific gap between those two things, and that gap is where most scaling companies lose years of momentum.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think they have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit. There is a difference, and it is costing them.

Gartner recently flagged something that should stop every Chief Sales Officer cold: AI is saving your team time, but that time is not automatically converting into revenue. Someone has to own the translation from efficiency to growth. If that is not happening at the leadership level, you are funding productivity theater.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They confuse activity metrics with pipeline health. Calls and demos are not a strategy.

2. They build compensation plans around last year's market, not next year's targets.

3. They treat sales process as a training issue instead of a leadership issue.

At $50M, you can survive on relationships and hustle. At $150M, that same approach becomes your ceiling.

The companies that scale past $200M treat sales strategy as a standing agenda item in the boardroom, not a quarterly slide deck.

So here is the question: who in your organization owns your sales strategy, and when did they last rebuild it from scratch?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Gartner makes a point that every scaling company should print and post on the wall: AI time savings will not drive revenue unless sales leaders actively intervene.

This is exactly what we see with companies in the $50M to $200M range. They invest in tools. They train the team. They watch efficiency numbers climb. Then they wonder why the revenue line does not follow.

The gap is almost never the technology. It is the absence of a deliberate sales strategy that connects efficiency gains to growth outcomes.

If your CSO cannot explain in one sentence how your current sales motion converts saved time into closed revenue, you have a strategy problem, not a technology problem.

At Autobahn, this is the exact conversation we have with leadership teams before anything else moves.

Read the Gartner piece here and ask yourself if your team is intervening or just adopting: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg

post3.text:
Gartner is now telling sales leaders what our chapter authors Deb and Brandon have seen on the ground for years: technology does not fix a broken sales strategy. It just accelerates the results of whatever strategy you already have, good or bad.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business, titled "Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation," hits this directly. The chapter title alone should make any founder or CEO a little uncomfortable. It is designed to.

Deb and Brandon lay out why most growing companies are unknowingly writing checks to the competition every single quarter, and what a real sales strategy actually looks like at the $50M to $500M stage. The insight is not what most leaders expect.

If your current sales approach was built when you were half your current size, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every day your company runs without a documented, leadership-owned sales strategy, you are making an involuntary donation to a competitor. At $50M, that is a manageable problem. At $150M, it is a growth ceiling. And no amount of AI tooling, new hires, or sales training closes the gap until leadership treats sales strategy as a core business asset, not a departmental concern.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ companies are invisible and they have no idea.

They have a logo, a website, maybe a tagline. They call it a brand. It is not a brand. It is wallpaper.

Ulta Beauty's CMO recently spoke about how the company deliberately connects brand identity to every customer touchpoint across channels. That is not a marketing tactic. That is a business decision made at the leadership level.

Here is what that means for scaling companies:

1. Your brand is not what your design agency delivered. It is what your customers feel when they interact with you at every level of the business.

2. Omnichannel is not a digital strategy. It is a consistency strategy. If your brand behaves differently in a sales call than it does on your website, you have a brand problem masquerading as a marketing problem.

3. The companies that win from $50M to $500M are the ones where the CEO treats brand as a growth lever, not a communications function.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If your company disappeared tomorrow, would your market actually notice?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive digs into how Ulta Beauty's CMO thinks about blending brand building with omnichannel marketing. Worth reading if you lead a company with serious growth targets.

The insight that stood out to us: Ulta does not treat brand and performance marketing as separate functions pulling in opposite directions. They treat them as one system.

For companies scaling past $50M, this distinction matters more than most leaders realize. At that size, you can still outspend your way to short-term revenue. But the companies that reach $500M and beyond have built a brand that does work their sales team cannot do alone.

If your marketing budget and your brand strategy are managed in separate rooms by separate people with separate goals, that is a scaling problem waiting to surface.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
Ulta Beauty's approach to brand consistency across every customer touchpoint is exactly the kind of thinking that belongs in a boardroom conversation, not just a marketing meeting.

In Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?", authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West tackle a question that makes a lot of senior leaders uncomfortable: Does your brand actually communicate something distinct, or does it just exist?

One of the chapter's sharper observations is that at the $50M to $500M growth stage, vague branding is not a creative problem. It is a revenue problem. The companies that scale successfully have learned to make their brand felt, not just seen.

There is a framework in this chapter that will change how you evaluate every marketing dollar you spend. We will leave it at that for now.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem in disguise.

As companies push past $50M, the instinct is to scale headcount to match revenue targets. But SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends points to something different: the leaders pulling ahead are hiring with precision, not volume. They know exactly what gap they are filling and why it matters now.

Here is what that looks like in practice:

First, role clarity before recruitment. If your hiring manager cannot articulate the specific outcome this person owns in 90 days, the seat will be wrong before it is filled.

Second, talent decisions are business model decisions. Who you hire, and when, shapes your operational ceiling more than any process improvement.

Third, the cost of a slow hire is real, but the cost of a wrong hire at the leadership level is a multiplier on every bad decision that follows.

Scaling from $50M to $500M is not a headcount race. It is a judgment race.

What is the one role at your company that, if filled perfectly today, would change everything in the next 12 months?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM titled "Precision Over Scale: The New Rules of Hiring in 2026" makes a case that companies are finally moving away from mass hiring and toward deliberate, high-fit talent acquisition.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth range, this is not a trend. It is a survival skill.

At that scale, one misaligned hire in a senior seat does not just slow you down. It reorganizes your priorities for the next 18 months while you manage around the gap.

Autobahn works with leaders navigating exactly this. The companies that scale cleanly treat every key hire as a strategic investment with a defined return, not a slot to fill on an org chart.

Read the SHRM piece and ask yourself: does your current hiring process reflect this level of precision?

The chapter is called The Talent Engine, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West. Together they lay out what it actually takes to build a people strategy that can carry a company from $50M to $500M without breaking under its own weight.

One thing Caleb, Darla, and Yasmin make clear: talent is not a department. It is an operating system. And like any system, if it is not designed to scale, growth will expose every crack in it faster than you expect.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not mean better decisions. For most $50M+ companies, they mean slower ones.

Leaders at this stage often believe that measuring more things creates more clarity. It creates noise. Oracle NetSuite recently outlined 11 hospitality-specific KPIs worth tracking, and the discipline behind that industry's approach reveals something most scaling companies miss: the metrics you cut matter as much as the ones you keep.

Here is what business leaders at the $50M to $500M range should consider:

1. A KPI without an owner is decoration. If no one is accountable for moving a number, that number will not move.

2. Lagging indicators tell you what happened. If your dashboard is full of them, you are always managing the past.

3. The right number of KPIs for a leadership team is probably fewer than seven. Anything beyond that competes for attention rather than directing it.

The companies that scale cleanly are not the ones tracking everything. They are the ones ruthlessly focused on the few numbers that actually drive the business forward.

What is the one KPI your leadership team would fight hardest to keep if you could only choose three?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com walked through 14 tools designed to help businesses track KPIs more effectively. Good tools. But here is what the article does not address: the tool is not the problem most scaling companies have.

At Autobahn, we work with companies moving from $50M to $500M and beyond. The pattern we see is not a lack of dashboards. It is leadership teams drowning in data while starving for direction. Adding another tracking tool to a broken measurement strategy speeds up the confusion.

Before you invest in new software, get ruthlessly clear on which metrics actually connect to your growth goals. The infrastructure should follow the strategy, not lead it.

If your team is evaluating KPI tools, start here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Business.com recently published a roundup of tools for tracking KPIs. It is a practical list. But the harder conversation is the one that comes before you open any tool: are you measuring the right things at all?

Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is called Death by KPIs. Authors Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall tackle this exact trap. Scaling companies often inherit a metrics culture built for a smaller operation, and then layer more dashboards on top of it as they grow. The chapter challenges leaders to audit not just what they measure, but why those numbers made it onto the list in the first place.

The insight that will stick with you: more visibility into the wrong numbers is not an advantage. It is a liability with a great interface.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling companies do not have a data problem. They have a focus problem disguised as a data problem. When leadership teams track 30 KPIs, they are effectively tracking none. This piece breaks down why the $50M to $500M growth stage is where measurement strategies either sharpen your execution or quietly sabotage it, and what to do instead.

post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong. They treat it like a faster search engine instead of a second brain running in parallel.

Bloomberg recently surveyed CEOs on their top AI productivity moves. The pattern was clear: the leaders getting the most out of AI are not using it to automate tasks. They are using it to multiply judgment.

Here is what that looks like at the $50M+ level:

1. AI does not replace your thinking. It surfaces what you are missing before a decision gets made. Leaders who build that into their daily workflow catch blind spots faster than their competitors.

2. The productivity gap between AI-literate executives and everyone else is widening faster than most boards realize. This is not a future problem.

3. The companies scaling past $100M right now have one thing in common: they treat AI adoption as a management discipline, not an IT initiative.

The question is not whether your team is using AI. It is whether your leadership is using it well enough to matter.

What does AI fluency actually look like in your executive team today?

post2.text:
A recent piece in The New York Times explored a growing trend among busy executives: deploying AI versions of themselves to handle routine interactions and keep decisions moving without their constant presence.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, and this cuts to something we see constantly. Leadership bandwidth is the hidden ceiling. When the person at the top is the bottleneck, growth stalls regardless of how strong the rest of the business is.

AI tools that extend executive presence are not a novelty. For scaling companies, they are fast becoming a structural advantage.

If you lead a company in that growth corridor, ask yourself: where is your time the bottleneck, and what would it take to remove that constraint?

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail your company's growth are not the incompetent ones. They are the highly capable ones who have quietly convinced themselves they do not belong in the room.

Imposter syndrome does not go away when you hit $50M in revenue. According to Forbes Australia, it actually intensifies as high achievers climb higher. The stakes grow. The visibility grows. And so does the internal narrative that someone is about to figure out the truth.

Here is what that costs scaling companies specifically:

First, leaders with unchecked imposter syndrome avoid bold decisions. They optimize for not being wrong instead of being right.

Second, they under-delegate because they do not trust that others see their authority as legitimate. That bottleneck kills growth at exactly the moment you need velocity.

Third, they rarely ask for help, which means the executive team operates on incomplete information and misaligned priorities.

The question worth sitting with: Is your leadership team making growth decisions from confidence, or from the fear of being exposed?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes Australia makes a point that should matter to every CEO scaling past $50M: imposter syndrome does not fade with success. It follows high achievers all the way to the top.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this play out in very concrete ways. Leaders who built companies to $50M often struggle to see themselves as the person qualified to take it to $500M. That gap between their actual capability and their self-perception creates hesitation at exactly the moments that require conviction.

For scaling companies, this is not a soft issue. It shows up in stalled hiring decisions, avoided investor conversations, and leadership teams that never fully align because the person at the top is not operating from a stable foundation.

If your growth has plateaued, it is worth asking whether the ceiling is strategic or psychological.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it tackles something most business books completely ignore: the psychological weight that comes with leading a company through serious growth.

Authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, the chapter confronts imposter syndrome not as a personal quirk but as a genuine organizational risk. One of the core insights is that the very traits that drove a leader to $50M can become the source of their deepest self-doubt at scale. Success, paradoxically, can make the internal noise louder.

What the chapter reveals is that the leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who eliminated that doubt. They are the ones who learned what to do with it.

post1.text:
The goal is not work-life balance. The goal is a life you actually designed.

Most leaders scaling past $50M are so focused on the business that they never stop to ask what they're building toward personally. Then the exit happens, the milestone gets hit, and the emptiness catches them off guard.

Research from Entrepreneur confirms this pattern: the majority of founders who sell report regret within a year, not because the deal was bad, but because they had no vision for what came next.

Three things high-growth leaders get wrong about life planning:

1. They treat personal goals as a reward for business success, not a parallel track to it.
2. They confuse financial independence with fulfillment.
3. They wait until a transition forces the conversation instead of having it during the build.

The leaders who navigate scale without losing themselves are the ones who treat life design with the same rigor they bring to a strategic plan.

What would your life look like if the business hit every number you set, starting tomorrow?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced with Morgan Stanley, lays out a financial and emotional roadmap for entrepreneurs navigating life after a business sale. It is worth reading.

But here is what it does not address: most founders at the $50M to $500M stage are not thinking about post-exit identity until it is too late to prepare for it.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Leaders spend years scaling with precision and then arrive at a liquidity event with no personal framework for what follows. The financial plan exists. The life plan does not.

If you are in a growth phase right now, the time to build that framework is today, not at the closing table.

Read the full Fortune piece here and then ask your leadership team what your collective answer is to the question it raises.

75% of founders regret selling within a year. That number should stop every scaling leader cold.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles exactly this. Written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter is not about slowing down. It is about building a personal life plan with the same intentionality you bring to your business plan.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the leaders who thrive through scale and beyond are the ones who define what winning looks like outside the business before they need that answer.

Most companies we work with have a strategic roadmap. Very few have a personal one running alongside it. That gap is where regret lives.

posts.blog_hook: Most $50M+ leaders have a five-year plan for their business and no plan at all for their life. That gap does not show up on a P&L, but it shows up everywhere else. The data on founder regret post-exit is not a cautionary tale about deal structure. It is a story about what happens when you scale a company without ever designing the life it was supposed to fund.
